turns.content: Hey. I need a second pair of eyes on something. Julian moved out while I was at a work thing out of town—left a note saying dropping his key ends his obligation. Our lease has three months left at $2,800 total. I keep reading Clause 14 and it seems clear: joint and several liability until the lease ends unless we all sign a Release and Assignment Addendum. Am I reading that right? Because the shock of walking into an empty apartment and finding a note is still settling, and I want to be sure before I do anything else.

**Based on your description of Clause 14, your reading appears correct:** moving out and returning a key would not, by themselves, release Julian from the lease. His note states his position; it does not establish that his obligation has ended.

Two distinctions matter:

- **Liability to the landlord:** “Joint and several liability” generally means the landlord can seek the full unpaid rent from either tenant—not just each tenant’s share—subject to the lease and applicable law.
- **Liability between you and Julian:** What he owes you depends on your rent-sharing agreement and local law. Joint and several liability alone does not establish a 50/50 split.

Three months at $2,800 is **$8,400 in scheduled rent remaining**, not necessarily the amount ultimately recoverable from either of you. A valid release, replacement tenancy, statutory termination right, or applicable duty to mitigate losses could affect that amount.

I haven’t seen the clause, the rest of the lease, or your jurisdiction’s rules, so this is a provisional interpretation, not a definitive legal conclusion.

**My recommendation:** preserve his note, messages, lease, and payment records; ask the landlord in writing whether any release, assignment, or termination has been executed; and have a local tenant adviser or lawyer review the actual clause before you make a payment demand. Do not assume his departure reduces what the landlord can require from you.

ok. so i'm not wrong about the clause. that helps. i keep replaying his note in my head: 'dropped the key off, you're set, i'm out.' as if a key return rewrites a contract.

what i keep coming back to: he's not even pretending this is about hardship. he just decided he's done, and the financial part should disappear because he wants it to.

Based on the clause as you described it, **returning the key alone would not end his lease obligation**. That interpretation still needs confirmation against the full lease and local law.

His note presents his departure as settled without explaining how the remaining rent will be handled. It does **not** establish whether he is facing hardship, misunderstands the lease, or intends to avoid payment. The financial obligation and his reasons are separate questions.

**My recommendation:** confirm the release status with the landlord, then ask Julian in writing how he intends to cover his agreed share of the remaining rent. Keep that exchange focused on the lease, your payment arrangement, and dates—not on proving his motive.

Here's the math that's keeping me up: $1,400 a month, three months left, $4,200 total. My savings are $5,200. Covering his share alone leaves me with $1,000 to my name—and that's if nothing goes wrong. I'm protecting both our credit records by paying, and he's just gone.

**Your arithmetic is correct:** covering an additional $1,400 for three months would cost $4,200, leaving $1,000 of your $5,200 savings—before any other withdrawals or unexpected expenses. That would use about **81% of your savings**.

Paying the full rent on time would prevent a rent shortfall. It does not guarantee protection of either credit record; credit consequences depend on reporting, collections, and what happens afterward. Under the joint-and-several clause you described, paying would also protect you against an unpaid-rent claim from the landlord.

The immediate financial exposure is separate from whether you can recover Julian’s share. Even if he owes you $4,200 under your rent-sharing agreement, **you cannot budget as though reimbursement is certain or immediate**.

Before committing that much of your savings:

- **Confirm with the landlord in writing** whether any release exists and what approved replacement-tenant or early-termination options are available. Don’t assume either option releases you without written terms.
- **Request Julian’s payment in writing**, identifying the agreed $1,400 monthly share and the remaining due dates. Preserve evidence of that agreement and any payments you cover.
- **Get local tenant-law advice before rent becomes overdue**, including advice about your potential reimbursement claim and how to reduce the remaining exposure.

**My recommendation:** plan around the possibility that Julian pays nothing, while promptly pursuing payment and a written arrangement that reduces your liability. Do not treat spending the entire $4,200 as inevitable before checking those alternatives.

so i need to talk to management. what exactly do i ask them? do i just say 'has any release or assignment addendum been executed,' or is there a gentler way to find out if they'll help me hold him to it?

**Ask about the lease status first, then management’s payment and replacement procedures.** Management may seek payment from either tenant under joint and several liability; it is not necessarily responsible for enforcing your rent-sharing agreement.

You can send:

> **Subject: Lease status and options for remaining term — [unit]**
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Julian told me he moved out and returned his key. I remain in the apartment, and the lease has three months remaining.
>
> My understanding of Clause 14 is that both tenants remain liable unless the required Release and Assignment Addendum is signed. Could you please confirm:
>
> - Has any release, assignment, termination agreement, or other change to the lease been executed? If so, please provide a copy.
> - Does management currently regard both of us as liable under the existing lease?
> - Can management contact both of us directly about the remaining rent obligations?
> - What options are available for an approved replacement tenant or early termination, including any fees and signatures required?
>
> I’m trying to clarify the lease status and address the remaining rent before a payment problem arises. Please respond in writing.
>
> Thank you,  
> [name]

This requests their help without assuming they can require Julian to pay exactly $1,400 rather than pursue either of you for the full balance.

**My recommendation:** send the written inquiry now. If you discuss it by phone, follow up with an email documenting their answers; do not treat a verbal assurance as a release or lease amendment.

thanks for laying that out. i'll send it tonight. but i keep circling back to the same thing: he walks away with nothing, and i'm the one protecting both of us from delinquency. anyone would do that, but it still stings.

You report that it still stings. The financial imbalance you’re facing is concrete: if Julian pays nothing and you cover the remaining rent, you would spend an additional $4,200.

**His departure does not establish that he leaves without liability.** Based on your description of the lease, he may remain liable even while you bear the immediate cash burden. Whether and when you could recover his share remains unresolved.

Paying the full rent would prevent a shortfall and protect your own position; it is not something everyone could or would do, and it does not erase any reimbursement claim you may have.

**My recommendation:** send management the inquiry tonight and keep a separate record of every payment you make toward Julian’s agreed share. Treat reimbursement as uncertain when planning your budget.
